full_judgment:
2. On an application filed by respondent No.1(hereinafter referred to as the Writ petitioner) under article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, Rule Nisi was issued by the High Court Division yin Writ Petition No.2669 of 2000 on 29.05.2000 calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why Sections 3, 4(KaKa), 4(Kha), 5, 6(Uo), 7 and 11 of the Rangamati Hill District Local Government Council (Amendment) Act, 1998 (Act- No.9 of 1998), Khagrachari Hill District Local Government Council (Amendment) Act, 1998 (Act 10 of 1998) and Bandarban Hill District Local Government Council (Amendment) Act, 1998 (Act 11 of 2998)(hereinafter referred to as Acts, 9, 10 and 11 of 1998), section 15(Kha) of Acts 9 and 10, section 14(Kha) of Act -11 , section 28 of Acts 9 and 10 of 1998 section 27 of Act 11 of 1998, section 29 of Acts 9 and 10 of 1998, section 28 of Act 11 of 1998, section 31 of Acts 9 and 10 of 1998, section 30 of Act 11 of 1998, section 34 of Acts 9 and 10 of 1998, section 33 of Act 11 of 1998, section 25 of Acts 9 and 10 of 1998, section 24 of Act 11 of 1998, sections 5(2), 5(8), 7 and 40 of the Chittagong Hill Tracts Regional Council Act, 1998 (Act 12 of 1998), sections 4(4), 5(1) and (2) of Acts 19, 20 and 21 of 1989 and Act 12 of 1998 should not be declared unconstitutional and void. 

 4. As it appears from the writ petition, the writ-petitioner stated facts therein tracing back to the history of pre-liberation period leading to the formation of Chittagong Hill District comprising the eastern hilly areas of the then Chittagong District by the British Colonial Government in 1860, then enacting the Chittagong Hill Tracts Regulation, 1900 (Regulation No.1 of 1900) (hereinafter referred to as the CHT Regulation, 1900) and framing of Rules thereunder, but the questions as to the constitutionality of the sections of Acts 9, 10, 11 and 12 of 1998 and Acts 19, 20 and 21 of 1989 having been called in question before the High Court Division and dealt With by it, we are not required to state the whole facts except the facts and the laws relevant for the disposal of these two leave petitions. Therefore, the facts stated in the writ petition and the relevant connected laws which are necessary for disposal of the questions posed in the leave petitions are stated herein below: 

 5. More than 20 years ago, that is, in 1979 the writ-petitioner went to Rangamati and after being settled he has been residing there permanently with his wife, children and other members of his family. The writ-petitioner is a businessman by profession and is a conscious citizen of the country. The writ-petitioner is very much aggrieved by the passing of Acts 9, 10 and 11 of 1998 as certain provisions of these Acts have affected his right of franchise, right to purchase, right to transfer property and the right to contest in various elected posts. The writ-petitioner is further aggrieved by the provisions of Act 12 of 1998 in that it has effectively created an autonomous region being the Chittagong Hill Tracts (CHT) by dismantling the unitary character of Bangladesh. It has been asserted in the writ petition that the unitary character of the State constitutes the basic structure of the Constitution. The CHT consisting of three districts, namely, Rangamati, Bandarban and Khagrachari covers a total area of 5,138 square miles which is one tenth of the total territorial area of Bangladesh and is home to a population of about 10 lakhs which constitute 0.5% of the total population of Bangladesh. Full of natural resources, the Chittagong  Hill Tracts is a hilly area dotted by five valleys namely, Chengi, Mainee, Kornophully, Mantamuhuri and Sangu. Apart from Bengalees who had been living there for the last few centuries, the CHT is the home of 13 tribes, namely, Chakma, Marma, Triptua, Taichaya,  Riyang, Mro, Lusai, Pankher, Boom, Chak, Khumi, Ushai and Khiang. In 1900 important and far reaching changes in the administration of the CHT were made by the British  Governs at by enacting the Chittagong Hill Trace Regulation, 1900 and by framing Rules thereunder. The Regulation the Rules and Orders came to be collectively known as the Hill Tracts Manual. The CHT continued to be administered by the Hill Tracts Mammal. Pursuant to the Hill Tracts Manual the an came to be divided into three circles, namely, the Chakma Circle with headquarters at Rangamati, the Bomang Circle with headquarters at Bandorban, and the Mong Circle with headquarters at Manik Chari in Khagrachari. The head of the Circle is known as the Chief, popularly known as the 'Raja' or 'King'. These Circle Chiefs or Kings have always had a distinctive role to play in the administration of the CHT notwithstanding that the administration was formally run by the Deputy Commissioners and Sub-divisional Deputy Commissioners. Notably, though the CHT fell within the boundaries of the undivided province of Bengal, its administration by a different law as reflected in the Hill Tracts Manual led it to acquire the status of a 'Non-regulated District'. The Indian Independence Act 1947 (the Act 1947), enacted by the British Parliament on 18 July, 1947 created the two independent dominions, namely, India and Pakistan with effect from 15 August 1947. Section 2 of the Act, 1947 specified the territories of the two dominions. Accordingly, by operation of section 3 of the Act 1947, the province of Bengal as constituted under the Act, 1935 ceased to exist, and two new provinces known as East Bengal and West Bengal were constituted. 

 (d) A constitutional provision restricting the amendment of the CHT Regulation, 1900 and imposing a ban on Bengali settlement in the CHT. These demands were rejected outright by the Prime Minister who, on the contrary, argued for relinquishing such parochial and ethnic aspirations in favour of these being subsumed under a broader notion of nationalism to facilitate national integration. Upon the enactment of the Constitution, the CHT lost its former status of 

 7. Mr. M.N. Larma as a member of the Constituent Assembly, in a display of his rejection of this unitary character of the State refused to vote for the new Constitution as adopted in November 1972. A political mobilization of the tribal people had by then been already underway as evident in the formation in early 1972 of the PCJSS as a political front with Mr. M.N. Lama at the helm. Consequently, the Shanti Bahini an armed wing of the PCJSS was formed on 7 January 1973 and after August 1975 became a clandestine organization engaged in armed insurgency against the Government. Although in limited numbers, the Bengalese had been living in the Chittagong Hill Tracts for centuries, after the creation of Pakistan in 1947 their numbers began to increase for various reasons; the requirement of skilled and unskilled labours for Kaptai hydro-electric project, Chandroguna paper mill, various kinds of development works within the Hill. Tracts and so on, But the number of Bengali settlers increased significantly, during the three period; immediately after the war in 1965, the independence in 1971 and during the period from 1979 to 1982/83. With the approval of the Government during the period of 1979 to 1982/83 a large number of poor Bengali landless families from across Bangladesh had been rehabilitated in the Hill Tracts. This was disliked by the Shanti Bahini and they resisted it with arms. From 1983 no new settlement of the Bengalese has taken place. On 6th March, 1989 three identical laws, namely, Rangamati Hill District Local Government Council Act, 1989 (Act 19 of 1989), Khagrachari Hill District Local Government Council Act, 1989 (Act 20 of 1989) and Bandarban Hill District Local Government Council. Act, 1989 (Act 21 of 1989) (hereinafter collectively referred to as the Original Acts of 1989) were passed by the Parliament; by which local governments were established in the three Hill Districts under article 59 of the Constitution. These laws provided detailed provisions for the establishment and functioning of local government by the elected representatives of the people consisting of both the tribal people and Bengali settlers. On 2nd December, 1997, an Agreements was signed between NCCHT formed by the Government of Bangladesh and the PCJSS. On behalf of the Government of Bangladesh Mr. Abdul Hasnat Abdullah signed the Peace Accord in his capacity as the Convenor of the NCCHT Mr. Joytirindra Bodhipriya, otherwise known as Santu Larma, Signed the Peace Accord in his capacity as the Chairman, PCJSS. Mr. Abut Hasnat Abdullah had no authority under the Constitution to sign the Peace Accord on behalf of the Government of Bangladesh. On the basis of the said agreement, three identical laws, namely. Act Nos.9 of 1998, 10 of 1998 and 11 of 1998 were enacted which were passed by the Parliament on 24th May, 1998 by which certain provisions of the original Acts of 1989 were amended. On 3rd December, 1998, section 2 (kaka) of the impugned Act Nos.9, 10 and 11 of 1998 has been further amended by which a non-tribal permanent resident would now mean a person who is the owner of lawful land and who has a permanent address in a Hill District. Deletion of the words 'Local Government' from the long title and from sections 1(1), 2(Uo). 3 and 7 of the three original Acts of 1989. by sections 2, 3. 4(kha), 5, 6 and 7 of the impugned Acts have prima facie taken the Rangamati, Khagrachari and Bandarban administrative units outside the purview of Local Government as enunciated in Part IV, Chapter III, of the Constitution and, therefore, voilative of articles 1, 7, 59 and 60 of the Constitution. Sections 6(Ume), 11 and 2(kaka) of the impugned Act are also violative of articles 27, 28(1) and 31 of the Constitution Section 15(kha) of the impugned Acts amending section 32 of the original Acts of 1989 giving preference to the tribal people in the employment of class II and III employees of the Council for an indefinite period is violative of articles 27 and 29 of the Constitution. Not only that, according to the amended provisions, the Government would not be able to employ persons in the other posts of the Council without first consulting the Council which is unconstitutional inasmuch as it has curtailed the executive power of the Government in derogation of article 133 of the Constitution. Section 28 of Act Nos.9, 10 and section 27 of Act No.11 of 1998 are discriminatory against the Bengali settlers and, therefore, offends articles 27 and 29 of the Constitution. The Omnibus restrictions imposed by the new section 64 on transfer of land without prior permission from the Council is unreasonable and violative of articles 42 and 144 of the Constitution. The new section 67 is violative of articles 1, 7(1) and 55(2) of the Constitution inasmuch as this section brings the Council at per with the Executive Government of the country which is against the concept of Unitary Government. 

 8. The repeal of section 70 from the original Acts by which the Government's power of delegation of its functions under the Act to any functionary has been abolished, has put fetter on the normal functioning of the Executive Government and is, therefore, unlawful and unconstitutional. On 24th May, 1998, the Parliament also passed Act 12 of 1998 creating a Regional Council consisting of three Hill Districts of Rangamati, Khagrachari and Bandarban, such Council is to be headed by a Chairman and members elected in accordance with the previsions of the Act. The concept of Regional Council is a concept which is incompatible, and inconsistent with the Constitution because it violates articles 1, 7 and 59 of the Constitution and negates unitary character of the State. The Regional Council has, in fact, created an autonomous area of Chittagong Hill Tracts by practicing fraud upon the Constitution. Sections 5(2) and 5(8) read with section 7 of Act 12 of 1998 which disqualify a person of non-tribal origin to become the Chairman of the Regional Council is discriminatory and violates articles 27 and 28(1) of the Constitution. Section 40 of Act 12 of 1998 effectively nullifies control of the executive Government of the Republic over the Regional Council to a mere advisory body even in case of violation of the Constitution or any other existing laws of the Country. Sections 4(4), 5(1) and (2) of Act Nos.19, 20 and 21 of 1989 which disqualify a person of non-tribal origin to become the Chairman of the Rangamati, Khagrachari and Bandarban Hill Districts Council is unconstitutional inasmuch as it is violative of articles 27, 28(1) and 31 of the Constitution. The repeal of sections 51 and 52 from the original Acts of 1989 by which central Government's power of control over, and investigation into, the functions of the Council have been abolished, is violative of articles 1, 7(1) and 55(2) of the Constitution. The various sections of Acts 9, 10 and 11 of 1998 and the creation of the Regional Council by Act 12 of 1998 not only violate the various provisions of the Constitution but also destroy the basic structures of the Constitution, namely; the unitary character of the State. The impugned Acts purport to create a territorial unit which eventually may claim the stains of a federating unit thereby destroying the very fabric of unitary Republic. In other words, by sowing the seeds of regionalism, the next step can be dismantling the fabric of the Republic. 

 9. The writ petition was contested by Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Law, Justices and Parliamentary Affairs (the petitioner in the Petition for. Leave to Appeal No.1847 of 2010) by filing an affidavit-in-opposition contending, inter-alia, that the writ petition filed by the writ-petitioner was misconceived, malafide, motivated and was filed for collateral purpose and, as such, the same was liable to be rejected. All the apprehensions made in the writ petition by way of submissions were baseless and untenable in law and on such apprehensions the writ petition could not be entertained. Peace Accord was signed and executed to facilitate the public interest in general, specially the people living in the Chittagong, Hilt Tracts in order to bring peace and harmony in the said region of Bangladesh so that the tribal and non-tribal people of Bangladesh  living in the said area could co-exist there. It was also done to give effect to the constitutional mandates for advancement of backward sections of the population and establishment of efficient local government institutions. The writ petition involved political and disputed question of facts and, as such, the same could not be reviewed by the High Court Division as it purported to challenge the execution, signing and implementation of the Chittagong Hill Tracts Accord, 1997 dated 02.12.1997 (hereinafter referred to as the Peace Accord). Peace Accord was enacted taking into account the then political situation which existed in the Chittagong Hill Tracts and, as such, that cannot be the subject matter of judicial review of this Court. The writ petition was also bad for defect of party as the appropriate parties against whom specific allegations were made, were not impleaded and the Rule was liable to be discharged on that ground alone. The petitioner was not a person aggrieved by the impugned provisions of Acts 9, 10, 11 and 12 of 1998. The Peace Accord neither violated any of the fundamental rights nor any other rights of the petitioner as guaranteed under the Constitution. The petitioner had no reason to be aggrieved by the provisions of Act 12 of 1998. The writ petition was filed with malafide intention and with political motive to disrupt the existing ethnic and communal peace and harmony in the Chittagong. Hill Tracts and to destabilize the region. It was not correct that the petitioner normally resides within the Rangamati District. The provisions of Act 12 of 1998 have not created autonomous region of Chittagong Hill Tracts and dismantled the unitary character of Bangladesh. There are absolutely no fetters on the petitioner's franchise, as his right to vote or to stand in the parliamentary elections and for elections to Union, Upazila and Municipal Councils etc. in the CHT, has not been adversely affected in any way. There is no bar against the elections to the Hill District Councils and election to the CHT Regional Council in accordance with the provisions of the impugned Acts 9, 10, 11 and 12 of 1998, if he can qualify as a permanent resident of the district in which he resides which is a qualification and norm for election to any local government body in Bangladesh under the relevant, laws. None of the provisions of the above Acts led to the creation of an autonomous region or dismantled the unitary character of the Republic, as neither the CHT, nor any of its three constituent districts, have been created into anything even vaguely resembling a federal unit, which would have clearly defined autonomous legislative, executive and judicial authority of the federal government and of the provincial governmental, which is not the case of the CHT institutions under references. 

 10. Respondent No.3 (petitioner in Leave Petition No.1891 of 2010) also contested the Rule by filing an affidavit-in-opposition stating, inter-alia, that the statements made about the settlement of poor Bengalees, which was disliked by the Shanti Bahini and the latter resisted it with arms, has no bearing to this writ petition. Mr. Abul Hasnat Abdullah, convenor of the NCCHT, had the authority to sign the Agreement and Jotindra Budhiprio Larma signed the Agreement in is actual capacity as the Chairman of PCJSS, The parliament having approved the Accord, the question of validity of authority of Mr. Abul Hasnat Abdullah to sign the same has no relevance. Khagrachari, Bandarban and Rangamati are all districts and are, therefore, administrative units under article 152 of the Constitution. Khagrachri, Bandarban and Rangamati being administrative units the provisions of article 59 of the Constitution are still attracted. The sum and substance of the contentions raised by respondent No.3 in the affidavit-in-opposition that none of the amendments as brought in the impugned Acts is violative of articles 7(1), 27, 28, 29, 31, 49, 55(2), 59, 60, 133 and 144 of the Constitution. The amendments have been brought in the impugned Acts to promote the interest, to secure participation of the local people in the Local Government, to secure adequate representation in the service of the Republic and to protect the properties of the backward sections of the citizens of Bangladesh. Local Government has been conceived of on the principle of gradual development of self-governing institutions with a view to progressive realization of responsible Government. Article 60 of the Constitution specially states that for the purpose of giving effect to the provisions of article 59 Parliament can confer powers on the local government bodies and the new section 67 of the 1989 Act enhances the concept of local government by providing for coordination. Local Government is meant for management of local affairs by locally elected persons and the repeal of section 70 enhances this  objective. The Regional Council is directly under the control of the Government of Bangladesh and hence its establishment does not in any way derogate the unitary character of the State. Act 12 of 1998 does not contain any provision inconsistent with articles 59 and 60 of the Constitution. Reservation of electoral posts pursuant to article 28(4) is Permissible, under the Constitution. The allegation that section 40 of Act 12 of 1998 nullifies control of the executive over the Regional Council to a mete advisory body even in case of violation of the Constitution is a wilful misreading of the Act inasmuch as section 41 of the Act categorically confers on the Government the power to cancel a Council if it considers that the latter has not been able to carry on its duty and is acting in contravention of public interest or in any way is abusing the power given to it. Moreover, the executive retains the final power of Cancellation of the Council under section 53 of the Acts. 

 12. Mr. Mahbubey Alam learned Attorney General, appearing in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.1847 of 2010 has contended that the Chittagong Regional Council Act, 1998, as enacted by the Parliament, in no way, violates the concept of the unitary character of the State He has further contended that a close reading of the various provisions of the said Act would show that the same has been enacted keeping the full control of the Government upon the Regional Council as a statutory public authority created for the purpose of facilitating local Government in the Chittagong Hill District Area. He has further contended that in construing that Regional Council Act offends the provisions of articles 59 and 60 of the Constitution, the learned Judges totally misconceived the said articles as well as the principle of law enunciated by this Division in the case of Kudrat-E-Elahi Panir. The learned Attorney General has further contended that the amendments as made by the impugned Acts being Nos.9, 10 and 11 of 1998 in no way offend the provisions of articles 1, 7, 27, 28(1), 29 and 31 of the Constitution; therefore, the High Court Division was wrong in declaring the provisions of the impugned Acts as specifically mentioned in the Rule issuing order dated 29.05.2000 ultravires to the Constitution. Mr. Attorney General has further contended that the provisions in the impugned Acts have been brought to safeguard and promote the interest of backward section of citizens which has clearly been provided for in article 28(4) of the Constitution, therefore, the High Court Division was not justified in Chairman declaring those legislations, as ultravires to the said provisions of the Constitution. The learned Attorney General by referring to articles 1, 7, 9,14, 27, 28(4), 29(3), 31, 59 and 60 of the  Constitution vis-a-vis the amended provisions as incorporated in Act Nos.9, 10 1 and 11 of 1998 and the provisions of Act 12 of 1998 has lastly contended that the questions involved in the leave petition require interpretation of the said articles of the Constitution by this Apex Court and, as such, leave may be granted to consider the points as formulated in ground Nos. III-VIII of the leave petition. 

 I. whether the High Court Division erred in law in holding that the Regional Council Act is nothing but a mere colourable piece of legislation which is based on an apparent misconstruction of the Kudrat-E-Elahi Panir Case inasmuch as a statutory body like the Regional Council comprising of elected per sons and for the purpose of aiding and facilitating local government functions such a body would automatically and necessarily have to squarely fit within the four corners of articles 59 and 60 of the Constitution. The Regional Council does not purport to be a local government body but is a statutory public authority created for the purpose of facilitating local government in the CHT within the broader scheme of 'special measures' and/or 'affirmative action'. 

 II. whether the High Court Division manifestly erred in law in holding, without any basis, that the "Regional Council has the potential to eventually claim the status of a federating unit for the CHT thereby destroying the very fabric of a unitary Republic" inasmuch as the Regional Council Act in its preamble expresses "full and total allegiance to sovereignty and territorial integrity of Bangladesh". The Regional Council owes its existence to the wilt of the executive government and under the conditions stated in sections 40 and 41 is amenable to dissolution upon an 'executive order' without the involvement of any constitutional or legislative procedure and hence does not nearly resemble a federating unit and neither does it possess any potentiality 10 do so. 

 III. whether the High Court Division manifestly erred in law in holding that that sections 40 and 41 appear to be deliberate in their formulation to further underlying cause of the Regional Council Act to erode the unitarily of the State inasmuch as the Court failed to appreciate that under the Act the Council is directly under the control and super, vision of the Government. The Regional Council does not nearly resemble a federating unit and neither does it possess any potentiality to do so particularly since federating' units demand 'devolution of executive,  legislative and judicial powers of different regions to turn into Province ultimately. The finding of the High Court Division does not have any discernibly objective basis inasmuch as the unitary state comes in several-guises and cannot be equated with a mono-centric system of government. 

 IV. whether the High Court Division erred in law in holding that section 6 of the impugned HDC Acts requiring certificate of the. Circle Chiefs on the basis of certificate issued by the headman or the Union Parishad Chairman or thee. Pourashava Chairman as the case may be infringes the petitioner's right of franchise inasmuch as the petitioner or other non-tribal persons are not in anyway restricted from contesting or voting in the parliamentary or local government elections even without any certificate from the concerned Chiefs and even in the case of elections to hill district and regional Councils provided that he fulfills the reasonable criterion of residency in the area concerned which is an essential qualification for participating in local government  elections of all types within Bangladesh, he can participates in elections without discrimination and undue restrictions, the practice of issuing certificates by the Chiefs has been in place since the British period and has been routine administrative practice and Circle Chiefs issue certificates to tribals and non-tribals alike. It is common practice across democracies to require a 'property qualification' or a 'residency qualification' and, therefore, that is seen as a legitimate requirement which in no way circumscribes a persons rights of franchise and seeks to manifest the very essence of partaking in the determination of who would be accountable for the management of local affairs locally. 

 VI. whether in passing the impugned judgment and order the High Court Division failed to consider the spirit of the Preamble, articles 9, 11, 14, 28(4) and 29(3) of the Constitution which provides to promote local government, to guarantee the fundamental human rights and freedom and respect for dignity and worth of the human person, to emancipate the toiling masses the peasants, workers and backward sections of people from all forms of exploitation in the CHT and nothing shall prevent the state from making special provisions in favour of women, children and for advancement of the backward Sections of citizens.
